channel.title: Timeline on GrapheneFacts
channel.description: Recent content in Timeline on GrapheneFacts

item.description:
Evidence: Mixed; tag each row.

Twist / geometry

  • MIT/Harvard Nature (5 Feb 2025 note): first direct superfluid-stiffness measurement in magic-angle graphene; ~10× conventional expectation in that report; temperature dependence read as quantum-geometry.
  • Nature 637, 1084 (22 Jan 2025). Moiré-driven topological electronic crystals in twisted bilayer–trilayer graphene; ν = 1/4 with integer quantum anomalous Hall; Chern number switchable +1/−1.
  • Helical trilayer magnetism, Nat. Phys. (Jan 2025 MIT note).

Fridge stacks. Not powder.

Evidence: Named standards, papers, and RNS. Do not back-fill from a 2026 weekly without the 2024 artifact.

Standards

ISO/TS 80004-13:2024 (Sep 2024) replaces the 2017 vocabulary. Adds GR2M among other revisions. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Health primary

Andrews et al. 2024 — controlled graphene oxide inhalation in humans (NCT03659864). Form × route row, not a treatment claim. [[topics/health/form-route]]

Industry cash

  • Jun 2024 — Directa Plus ~£6.8–6.9 million at 18p.
  • 30 Apr — NanoXplore C$60 million RBC facility (debt).
  • Nov — Haydale ~£3.1 million + £0.5 million CLN.

[[topics/finance/raises-2015-2025]]

Evidence: Named papers and company notices. Flagship instrument names belong on the Commission page, not a blog paraphrase.

Twist / proximity

  • Zhou et al., Nature 613, 268 (2023). Bernal bilayer graphene + WSe₂: SC at zero field, Tc up ~10× vs the fragile ~30 mK window without WSe₂ in that comparison; density window ~8× wider. Only when the field pushes holes toward WSe₂ (Ising SOC story).
  • Su, Kuiri, et al., Nat. Mater. 22, 1332 (2023). Twisted double bilayer + WSe₂ superconducts in small pockets at 1.24° and 1.37°. TDBG without the dichalcogenide had been the missing cousin.

Still fridge stacks.

Evidence: Named papers and the Haydale RNS. “First order” headlines still need the order text.

Twist

  • Park / Cao / Jarillo-Herrero line, Nat. Mater. 21, 884 (2022) and the MIT “family” note: alternating-twist quadrilayer (and the five-layer cousin) host correlated and superconducting pockets near new magic angles (~1.68° class for ATQG). Family, not a SKU.
  • Kim et al., Nature 606, 494 (2022). STM/STS on magic-angle trilayer: reconstruction toward mirror-symmetric stacking; coherence peaks; doping window that looks like a gap-to-nodal crossover in that paper’s language.

Industry

13 Sep 2022 — Haydale ~£5.51 million. [[topics/finance/raises-2015-2025]]

Evidence: Well-supported for the Nature trilayer paper and for regulator ingredient lists. Fringe for covert-ingredient claims.

Twist

Cao, Park, Watanabe, Taniguchi, Jarillo-Herrero, Nature 595, 526 (2021). Magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene: superconductivity in in-plane fields >10 T, about 2–3× the conventional Pauli limit in that report; re-entrant SC at high field over a narrower density/displacement window. Not predicted from strong spin–orbit. Still three sheets in a fridge. arXiv 2103.12083 (22 Mar); journal 21 Jul.

Evidence: Named papers and the FGR close notice. First-post dates for rumor videos vary by platform.

Twist

  • Stepanov, Das, Lu, et al., Nat. Phys. 16, 926 (2020). Superconductivity in magic-angle bilayer can sit away from the correlated insulators; SC survives larger angle detuning. Competing-phases reading, not “doped Mott like cuprates only.”
  • Cao / Jarillo-Herrero 2020 Nature pair (same week MIT notes): mapping local twist disorder, and a four-layer magic-angle stack more sensitive to E and B than the bilayer. Still a fridge device.

Twisted trilayer Pauli-limit story is 2021. Do not collapse the years.

Evidence: Named 2019 papers. Plant openings stay on [[logs/companies]].

Twist follow-on

  • Yoo, Engelke, et al., Nat. Mater. 18, 448 (2019). Atomic reconstruction in twisted bilayer graphene; crossover near θc ≈ 1° from incommensurate moiré to commensurate domains with soliton walls.
  • Chen, Sharpe, Gallagher, et al., Nature 572, 215 (2019). ABC trilayer graphene / hBN moiré: Mott-like states at 1/4 and 1/2 filling below ~20 K; signatures of tunable superconductivity under a displacement field. Not magic-angle bilayer; a different stack.
  • Mid-2019 STM / spectroscopy cluster on magic-angle bilayer (Kerelsky, Xie, Jiang in Nature; Choi preprint) — maps the flat-band correlations the 2018 transport papers announced.

Still two sheets (or three) in a fridge. Not a tote.

Evidence: Well-supported Nature pair. Vendor claims stay their own class.

Twistronics

Cao, Fatemi, Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues, Nature 556 (2018):

  • 80–84 — correlated insulator at half-filling in magic-angle twisted bilayer (~1.1°).
  • 43–50 — unconventional superconductivity; Tc up to 1.7 K in that report; dome-shaped phase diagram compared to cuprates in the paper’s language.

This is two sheets, a twist, a fridge. It is not PureGRAPH in a tote. Log the idea (twist as a knob) on [[logs/theories]].

Evidence: ISO cover date and Abraham paper. The vocabulary does not certify a bag of powder.

Vocabulary

ISO/TS 80004-13:2017 — first edition September 2017 (ISO); IEC webstore date 14 November 2017. 21 pages. Lists terms for graphene and related 2D materials, production methods, properties, characterization. Withdrawn when 80004-13:2024 replaced it. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Membranes

Abraham, Vasu, Williams, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 12, 546 (2017). Physically confined GO laminates; interlayer d tuned ~9.8 Å to 6.4 Å. Ion permeation thermally activated; water less affected. Demo: 97% NaCl rejection in that confined stack. Continuation of Nair 2012, not a municipal plant.

Evidence: Named papers and Flagship dates. Tonnage announcements are not this page.

Policy

April 2016 — Graphene Flagship moves from ramp-up into the first Core project under Horizon 2020. That is a contract phase change, not a product launch. [[timeline/2013]]

Science

  • Ruffieux, Cai, et al., Nature 531, 489 (2016). Bottom-up zigzag-edge graphene nanoribbons on a surface; STS shows edge-localized states. Atomically precise edges in UHV, not a reel of ribbon.
  • Goykhman et al., Nano Lett. 16, 3005 (2016). On-chip silicon–graphene plasmonic Schottky PD; Flagship copy quotes 0.37 A/W at 1.55 µm with avalanche gain. Competes with SiGe in that demo, not a transceiver SKU.
  • Kawai et al., Science 351, 957 (2016). Graphene nanoribbons dragged on gold — superlubricity at 2–200 pN for 5–50 nm ribbons.

Standards weather

ISO/TS 80004-13 lands 2017. 2016 is committee year. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Evidence: Named papers and buildings. Sensor-in-the-brain language is motivation, not a clearance.

Science

  • Thomas et al., ACS Nano 9, 10909 (2015) — holey graphene as a molecular stencil on gold. [[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]]
  • Kim, Yu, Kim, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 10, 676 (2015). Electrically biased suspended graphene emits bright visible light. Hot electrons ~2,800 K localized because the substrate heat sink is gone; ~1,000-fold thermal-radiation efficiency vs on-SiO₂ mid-IR emitters in that comparison. CVD arrays shown. A lab emitter, not a display SKU.

Institutions

National Graphene Institute (Manchester) opens as a dedicated building.

Evidence: Well-supported papers and listing dates. Product pitches need their own primary.

Listing

April 2014 — Haydale AIM (HAYD). About US$11 million gross in contemporaneous copy; convert the sterling RNS when attaching it. Plasma-functionalization story, not a 4,000 t mill. [[topics/manufacturing/haydale]]

Photodetectors

  • Liu, Chang, Liu, Zhong, Nat. Nanotechnol. 9, 273 (2014). Double-layer graphene heterostructure phototransistor. Room-temperature visible-to-mid-IR; mid-IR responsivity >1 A/W in that report.
  • Koppens, Mueller, Avouris, Ferrari, Vitiello, Polini, Nat. Nanotechnol. 9, 780 (2014). Review of graphene / 2D / hybrid photodetectors — the field’s map after the 2013 waveguide cluster.
  • Cai, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. (2014) photothermoelectric THz detector: room-temperature THz class, speed claim vs then-existing room-temp THz parts. Still a lab detector.

These sit with 2013 waveguide PDs. None is a catalogue SKU.

Evidence: Commission / Chalmers for the Flagship. AIM notice for AGM. Photonics papers as named.

Flagship dates (do not collapse)

  • 28 January 2013: Graphene named a FET Flagship. Chalmers / Jari Kinaret. Initial ~30-month EC €54 million. GRAPHENE 604391.
  • 10–11 October 2013: kickoff at Chalmers. €1 billion over ten years is a programme class, not a 2013 deposit.

Photonics cluster

September 2013 Nature Photonics cluster (three independent groups in the same issue window):

Evidence: Well-supported device and membrane papers. Market slides stay forecasts.

Devices

  • Britnell et al., Science 335, 947 (2012). Vertical graphene / hBN or MoS₂ / graphene. Room-temperature on/off ~50 (hBN) and ~10,000 (MoS₂) in that prototype.
  • Levendorf et al., Nature 488, 627 (2012). Patterned-regrowth lateral graphene / hBN.
  • Furchi et al., Nano Lett. 12, 2773 (2012). Graphene in a Fabry–Pérot microcavity; absorption pushed above 60% in that geometry; responsivity quoted 21 mA/W. A cavity trick, not a packaged receiver.

Membranes

  • Nair, Wu, Jayaram, Grigorieva, Geim, Science 335, 442 (2012). Sub-micron GO films helium-tight but water almost unimpeded (≥10^10 faster than He in that report). Capillary / humidity story. This is GO laminate, not a 2004 flake with a hole punched in it.
  • Koenig / Bunch line, Nat. Nanotechnol. 7, 728 (2012). UV-oxidative pores in micrometre graphene; H₂, CO₂, Ar, N₂, CH₄, SF₆ leak rates vs effusion model. Lab sieve, not a plant membrane.

Theme

No gap, no CMOS twin. Honest near paths: RF, sensors, photonics, membranes, additives.

Evidence: Well-supported for the IBM device papers. Display ledes attached to a mixer are speculation.

RF

Wu, Lin, Bol, Jenkins, Xia, Farmer, Zhu, Avouris (IBM), Nature 472, 74 (2011) — top-gated CVD graphene RF FETs on diamond-like carbon; gates to 40 nm; f_T to 155 GHz. Different route from the 2010 SiC 100 GHz result.

Circuit

June 2011: IBM graphene frequency mixer on silicon (Science circuit paper). Mixing shown to about 10 GHz. First widely cited circuit, not a phone SoC.

Evidence: Well-supported for prize, Science FET paper, Nature Nanotechnology 30-inch film, and Nature graphene-on-hBN. Prize lectures are not product warranties.

Prize

5 October 2010: Nobel Prize in Physics to Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov “for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene.” Experiments, not the word, not Wallace, not Boehm. Longer note on the same year: this page is the year entry; the older short Nobel page was merged here.

Evidence: Well-supported for the cited papers. GHz and “wafer-scale” in headlines are not a radio product.

Process — copper CVD

Li, Cai, An, Kim, Nah, Yang, Piner, Velamakanni, Jung, Tutuc, Banerjee, Colombo, Ruoff, Science 324, 1312 (2009). Large-area graphene grown by CVD on copper foils, mostly monolayer, transferable. This is the process later fabs and foundries keep trying to industrialize. It does not erase wrinkles, grain boundaries, or transfer polymer residue.

Evidence: Well-supported that growth-on-metal work is underway. Area and uniformity claims need the original figures, not the abstract.

Documented science / process

  • Chemical vapor deposition on nickel and early metal catalysts produces few-layer films that can be transferred. Quality is not yet the later copper-monolayer story ([[timeline/2009]]).
  • Electrochemistry, epitaxial graphene on SiC, and liquid-phase work all run in parallel. There is no single “the graphene process.”

Industry

Patent activity on platelets, inks, and composites is visible. Distinguishing a platelet company from a CVD-film company is already necessary and often skipped in coverage.

Evidence: Well-supported for reviews and the existence of two material families. Performance numbers in press are often best-flake, not average-product.

Documented science

  • Geim and Novoselov, Nature Materials 6, 183 (2007) — the review most later citations treat as the field’s map.
  • Graphene oxide (Hummer’s, Brodie, Staudenmaier routes) and reduced GO are now a parallel literature with different defects, chemistry, and honesty requirements.

Claims in the air

“Stronger than steel, thinner than paper, better than copper” compilations spread. Those comparisons mix ideal monolayer calculations with bulk steel and bulk copper — true as textbook limits, misleading as product copy.

Evidence: Well-supported as a literature-year characterization. Individual “first transistor” headlines vary by definition (field-effect on a flake vs useful circuit).

Documented science

  • Raman spectroscopy (D, G, 2D/G′ bands) becomes the cheap fingerprint for layer number and disorder. Later work will warn that Raman alone does not certify a commercial powder as monolayer graphene.
  • Graphene oxide reduction papers accelerate. Chemists and physicists are still not using the same sample when they say “graphene.”
  • Early FET demonstrations on exfoliated flakes continue the 2004 geometry.

Commercial / program

University groups and a few startups talk transparent conductors as an ITO replacement. ITO replacement will remain a slide more than a market for years. Log specific firms only when a name and filing exist ([[logs/companies]]).

Evidence: Well-supported for the core experiments. Interpretations (“relativistic electrons in a pencil mark”) are pedagogy, not extra data.

Documented science

  • Novoselov, Geim, Morozov, Jiang, Katsnelson, Grigorieva, Dubonos, Firsov, Nature 438, 197 (2005) — two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene.
  • Zhang, Tan, Stormer, Kim, Nature 438, 201 (2005) — experimental observation of the quantum Hall effect and Berry’s phase in graphene.

Together with [[timeline/2004]], these papers are why Wallace’s 1947 bands ([[timeline/1947]]) stop being a graphite approximation and become a measured monolayer spectrum.

item.title: 2004 — Isolation at Manchester
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The experiment, without the myth layer

Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov, and collaborators isolate few-layer and monolayer graphene by mechanical cleavage from graphite — the “Scotch tape” method — transfer flakes onto oxidized silicon, and measure an electric-field effect in atomically thin carbon films.

Landmark: Novoselov et al., Science 306, 666 (2004), “Electric field effect in atomically thin carbon films.”

What made 2004 the inflection point was the combination:

item.title: 1962 — Boehm monolayers
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (with later historiographic argument about what “first graphene” means)

What Boehm’s group reported

Hanns-Peter Boehm and colleagues work from graphite oxide, reduce it, and report extremely thin carbon films, including flakes identified as monolayer. The tools are the TEM / diffraction lineage of mid-century surface and colloid carbon chemistry — not a Hall bar on SiO₂.

Geim and Novoselov have publicly pointed at this line as an experimental precursor. The usual careful wording is:

item.title: 1947 — Wallace band structure
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The paper-shaped object

P. R. Wallace calculates the electronic band structure of a single layer of graphite in order to understand bulk graphite. Near what are now called the Dirac points (the K and K′ corners of the honeycomb Brillouin zone), the bands are linear. Electrons look massless. That linear dispersion is the theoretical signature people now treat as graphene’s calling card.

Wallace is not writing science fiction about sticky tape. He is doing solid-state theory with a two-dimensional unit as the building block of a three-dimensional crystal.

item.title: Before 1900
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

What “before graphene” actually contains

People used graphite for centuries — marks on surfaces, lubrication, crucibles, later electrodes and moderator blocks. That is three-dimensional stacked carbon. The modern graphene story is not “humanity discovered carbon sheets in 2004.” It is: when did a single honeycomb sheet become an object you could isolate, identify, and measure as a 2D electronic system?

The 19th century answers a different question: when did chemists start taking graphite apart between the layers?

Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

Crystallography

Early 20th-century X-ray work settles graphite as stacked honeycomb sheets of carbon — a 3D crystal built from 2D units. That picture is what later lets Wallace treat one sheet as a Hamiltonian ([[timeline/1947]]).

Oxide line continues

Brodie-style oxidation does not freeze in 1859. Papers and “graphite oxide paper” products through the 1910s keep the chemical route alive. This is still lamellar oxide, not a gated monolayer device.

Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

1948 — Ruess and Vogt

Transmission electron microscopy on dried graphene-oxide (graphite-oxide) suspensions shows very thin, creased carbon films. Thickness is in the nanometre class. This is imaging of the oxide route, not a Hall bar.

1950s

Reduction chemistry, ever-thinner flakes, and arguments about how few layers you are actually looking at. The conversation is colloid and surface carbon, sitting next to growing graphite-moderator and electrode industries.

item.title: 1963-2003 — Name, epitaxy, near misses
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported historical papers. Not “graphene was invented in 2004” and not “2004 was nothing.”

Naming

Mid-1980s, often cited as 1986: Boehm, Setton, Stumpp and colleagues fix graphene as the systematic name for a single graphite sheet (graphite + -ene). The word is older in talk; this is the nomenclature paper trail. [[timeline/1962]] · [[guides/glossary]]

Epitaxy that is real and stuck

  • Metal surfaces: monolayer carbon on Ni, Ru, Pt and cousins through the 1960s–1990s surface-science literature (LEED, AES, later STM). Land, Michely, Behm-type STM on Ru is the picture people remember from the early 1990s.
  • SiC: Van Bommel, Crombeen, Van Tooren, Surf. Sci. (1975) — heating SiC sublimes Si and leaves carbon-rich layers. That is epitaxial graphene on a wafer, usually not a gated flake on SiO₂.

These layers matter. They are a different object from the 2004 transferred/exfoliated FET. [[timeline/2004]]

item.title: 2005–2009 — Dirac physics and a research gold rush
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

Science

  • 2005: Transport and spectroscopy lock in graphene carriers as massless Dirac fermions — Wallace’s picture on a real flake ([[timeline/1947]], [[timeline/2004]]).
  • Quantum Hall work, Raman fingerprints (D/G/2D), and early CVD on metals become community habits.
  • Citation explosion. Labs stand up graphene groups as a default, not a novelty.

Industry seeds

Early companies and patents around nanoplatelets, transparent conductors, composites. Specialist press (e.g. Graphene-Info from 2009) starts the weekly-vendor drumbeat that still shapes 2026 coverage. Log first appearances on [[logs/companies]] when a named firm or product line is documented.

item.title: 2011–2012 — Post-Nobel acceleration
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at program level

CVD on copper plus transfer methods become the default film story. Flexible electronics, RF transistors, and photonics demos multiply. EU policy talk hardens toward a Flagship ([[timeline/2013]]).

The era’s idea — graphene replaces silicon — collides with band gap, contact resistance, and uniformity. File that ideal on [[logs/theories]]. Do not treat a 2011 keynote as a 2026 product.

Next

[[timeline/2013]]

item.title: 2014–2019 — Roadmaps, pilots, early products
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at overview level

Powders/platelets and CVD films increase. Niches that actually ship something: composites, coatings, additives, thermal interface materials, conductive inks, sports-equipment demos. “Graphene” on a label is not a monolayer guarantee — ISO/IEC terminology fights start here.

Research attention partly shifts to van der Waals heterostructures and other 2D crystals. The stencil paper ([[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]], 2015) sits in this window: graphene as a process tool, not a silicon killer.

item.title: 2020–2025 — Industrialization and Flagship hangover
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at overview level

Flagship-era tallies of patents and products need primary-source checks. Energy storage, composites, sensors, EMI/thermal remain the sales deck. Occupational guidance tightens (banding, workplace studies) — see [[topics/policy/2026-09-16-niosh-graphene-exposure]].

2021 is also when the GO-in-vaccine / 5G cluster takes the form still logged on [[logs/conspiracies]] and [[recurrence/log]]. Real nanosafety papers and fringe overlays travel in the same news cycle. Keep them split.

Next

item.title: Pre-chemistry — graphite before laboratories
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at the level of mining and craft history; specific ancient identifications of “graphite vs molybdenite vs galena” are often later reconstructions.

What this page is

Before there is a chemist named Brodie, there is a slippery black solid people write with and grease with. They do not have the word graphene. They often do not even have a clean distinction between graphite and look-alike minerals.

This is the floor of the timeline. Monday posts can start here when the hook is “graphene is new; carbon sheets are not.”
